prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian-language prose oeuvre, rooted in lyric poetry, whose dense, patterned sentences build memory, the body and dream into a cumulative metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: My laureate preference is unchanged, but my citation has changed in scope. My test is whether a voice can be heard in the writing 'nowhere else'. On public knowledge of Blinding, the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy, and Solenoid, Cărtărescu meets it at sentence level. His work also joins the intimate, the bodily and the cosmic in one project of real intellectual depth. The chair's observation is right that all six of us preferring one writer is not evidence of merit. I have therefore tested the case against the open questions instead of resting on the opening result. Three points hold. First, the voice and the architecture are the two claims that public knowledge supports most concretely. Second, a career of several decades with a poetic origin suggests an oeuvre, not one standout book. Third, one named writer with a Romanian-language prose project is a clean attribution. Moving to a narrower citation follows from the exchange. Palm and Sem-Sandberg argued that the poetry is the thinnest-translated strand, and Sward and Palm argued that the formal architecture, not only the imagery, should be named. I accept both arguments. The citation should claim the prose project and its cumulative structure, and mention the poetry only as its origin. That is what the committee can defend through translation. On the chair's question about Adonis, I read the gap between him and Cărtărescu as a difference in the evidence available to us, not a finding that his poetry is lesser. I still regard him as a very close second on formal and linguistic achievement.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot remove is that Cărtărescu's effect depends on Romanian density, rhythm and syntax, and I know the work only through translation and secondary description. Length is not sustained quality. Olsson, Sward and Sem-Sandberg are right that a maximalist, recursive method can restate its motifs without deepening them. If expert reading of the later volumes showed restatement more than enlargement, the case for the central novels would weaken, and Adonis would deserve a closer look. The claim for equal quality across the whole corpus, including the early fiction and poetry, remains unestablished, which is why I narrowed the citation. Michon is my third ranking, and the breadth objection to him is a real cost to my own ranking. Intensity is a legitimate form of achievement, but a prize for a whole authorship needs enough evidence of range, and I find that evidence thinner for him than for Cărtărescu or Adonis. That is a difference of weighting, not a verdict on his sentence-level quality.

responses.point: Olsson says the effect lies in Romanian sentence rhythm and density, that the poetry and early fiction are unevenly translated, and that very long works make consistency hard to judge without full reading.
responses.response: I take the length caveat as an open evidential question and not a rhetorical one. I agree that size alone cannot count as sustained quality. In response to his concern and the chair's first question, I would ask the committee's readers to compare the openings and closing movements of the Orbitor volumes, and Solenoid, for whether later passages extend the early structures or only echo them. If expert reading showed echo without enlargement, I would reconsider the strength of my preference. I also concede his point that the effect rests on Romanian texture. This is why my citation now names the prose project and its architecture, which the committee can defend through translation, and not the sentence-level beauty it cannot verify.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg centres the citation on the prose project and treats the poetry as origin and context, because he cannot confirm the poetry is of equal weight. He also asks for expert reports on the Romanian prose.
responses.response: I move toward this on scope. In round 1 I wrote that the prose project recurs 'across genres', which claimed more for the poetry than the evidence supports. I now word the citation so that the poetry appears only as the root of the prose. I also agree that expert reports on the Romanian prose would turn a provisional preference into a firm one. If none are available, the committee should say openly that it is judging the prose through translation and secondary accounts. Where I differ slightly is on Adonis. The same expert-report problem applies to him, so it cannot be a reason to place him lower on merit. It is only a reason for caution about how confident any of us can be.

responses.point: Palm argues that recurring obsessions are not a weakness in themselves, and reads Blinding and Solenoid as an escalation of scale and structure while marking this as a judgment from public knowledge. She also would not oppose Adonis on literary grounds.
responses.response: I agree that returning to a few obsessions marks many strong oeuvres, so recurrence is not my objection. The question is whether each large work enlarges the project. Her reading of escalation is plausible, and I hold it as I hold my own, as a judgment from public knowledge and not from verified reading of the whole corpus. I also share her view that the citation should name the formal architecture. On Carson, my sixth place stands. Palm's argument that the invention carries emotional and intellectual weight is serious, but she has not yet shown which works and what citation scope would make her a first choice. The chair's sixth question asks the same of Palm, and I would be open to being persuaded by a precise answer.

responses.point: Sward holds her preference as provisional, depending on readers confirming that later volumes develop the early ones, and would want the citation to name the cumulative architecture and not only the visionary style.
responses.response: I agree with both conditions and have adopted the second in my citation. 'Cumulative metaphysical architecture' is intended to commit the committee to a claim that can be tested and, if the later work only restates the early work, falsified. I also accept her point that applying the age and timing exclusion equally to Adonis and Cărtărescu is the right discipline. I would add that provisionality should cut both ways. If we hold Cărtărescu to a test of sustained development, the same test of formal renewal across his career applies to Adonis, and we cannot yet apply it to the Arabic.

responses.point: Carlberg's citation names a prose and poetic oeuvre, and she says Adonis would have the stronger claim if Cărtărescu's prose proved to repeat its motifs without deepening them.
responses.response: I take the poetry in her citation seriously, since the lyric origin matters to the texture of the sentences. But the chair's second question asks what justifies including poetry given its thin translation coverage, and I cannot answer that from the evidence. I would keep the poetry as origin and not as a ground of the award. I agree with her conditional on Adonis, and I read it as consistent with mine. If the repetition risk is confirmed, the formal and linguistic case for Adonis becomes the stronger one. I would not say it is already stronger, because that also would be a claim beyond our evidence.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's Romanian rhythm, density and syntax survives translation, including Swedish translation, cannot be resolved from the supplied evidence.
Whether the later long works enlarge the project of the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid or restate its motifs remains open, and I hold my reading as a judgment from public knowledge only.
Whether the poetry and early fiction sustain the level of the major novels is unestablished because translation coverage is uneven, which is why I keep the poetry out of the grounds of the citation.

The strength of Adonis's prosodic, lexical and intertextual achievement in Arabic can be assessed only through translation and secondary accounts, so I cannot tell whether the gap with Cărtărescu is one of merit or of evidence.
Whether a compact oeuvre such as Michon's can support a whole-oeuvre prize depends on a standard the committee has not stated.
I have not independently read or verified the works, and corpus coverage beyond the two representative titles named for each writer rests on general public knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records that I joined the committee for 2021 together with Anne Swärd and was elected in the same 2019 renewal round. It records no personal or professional tie to Cărtărescu or any other shortlisted writer. My own historical and psychological fiction and my critical work are context, not evidence of a preference for any candidate. I assert no recusal, and conflicts are disclosed here but not adjudicated.
